The D.C. Circuit has, however, tried to rein in zone-of-interests analysis 
to some degree. In Twin Rivers Paper Company LLC v. SEC, 934 F.3d 607 (D.C. 
Cir. 2019). That court held that plaintiffs who do not fall within a statute’s 
direct beneficiaries must be those whose “interests coincide systemically, not 
fortuitously with those of intended beneficiaries.” The court applied this 
approach to find that paper companies did not have standing to challenge an 
SEC rule allowing electronic deUvery of financial reports. Id. at 616.
F. REMEDIES: THE QUESTION 
OF UNIVERSAL RELIEF
1. BACKGROUND
As we have seen, it is possible, either under the APA or a specific 
statutory review regime, to bring suit to challenge unlawful agency action 
or unlawful agency inaction. Assuming there is no bar to review and the 
challenger wins on the merits, what is the remedy?
As for challenges to unlawful agency action, the APA in § 706 says the 
“reviewing court shall * * * hold unlawful and set aside agency action, 
findings, and conclusions found to be” invalid for any of the familiar 
enumerated reasons (that the action is arbitrary or capricious, in excess of 
statutory authority, etc.). The APA in § 703 says the “form of proceeding 
for judicial review,” in the absence of an adequate specific statutory review 
proceeding, is “any applicable form of legal action, including actions for 
declaratory judgments or writs of prohibitory or mandatory injunction or 
habeas corpus.” Specific statutory review provisions often use similar 
language; for pedagogical purposes, we will focus on the APA’s provisions.
The common approach in recent decades, when a court finds agency 
action unlawful, has been for the court to (1) “set aside” the action, (2) 
“vacate” the action, or (3) “enjoin” the action’s implementation. Somotimfis 
the court says it is doing two or all three of these things at once. Courts 
have often spoken as if there is little to no difference between these three 
terms and often seem to use them interchangeably. Thus, the Supreme 
Court in a recent unanimous opinion offhandedly equated “enjoin” with 
“set aside.” CIC Services, LLC v. IRS, 141 S.Ct. 1582, 1590 (2021) (“a 
request in an APA action to ‘enjoin the enforcement’ of an IRS reporting 
rule is most naturally understood as a request to ‘set aside’ that rule”). And 
the D.C. Circuit in a leading case casually equated “injunction” with
